Hi Brandon,
You need to enclose your shiny bit in an "app" and then you it should work. I'll send something later that uses the leafletr package to build a stand-alone html map that you can then embed into your Rmd (and then print the whole thing to html, assuming you aren't needing shiny). It's kind of a slick way to have an interactive map in a stand-alone slide presentation/html (so you don't need R to run/open).

Anyway, code below should work:

## Trialing {.columns-2}

  - Trialing
  - Imaging
  - Image Analysis

```{r, eval=T, echo=F,  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# polygon map
library(shiny)
library(htmlwidgets)
library(dplyr)
library(leaflet)
library(maps)

# need to embed in an app to use in slide show
shinyApp(
  ui = fluidPage(leafletOutput('MAP')),
  server = function(input, output) {

  map <- leaflet() %>%
      addTiles(group = "OSM") %>%  # Add default OpenStreetMap map tiles
      addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "ESRI Aerial") %>%
      addMarkers(lng=-121.8008111, lat=38.6295194, popup="Panel 1") %>%

      # add controls for basemaps and data
      addLayersControl(
        baseGroups = c("ESRI Aerial", "OSM"),
        options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE))

    # generate final map and output
    output$MAP = renderLeaflet(map)
  },
  options=list(height="500px")
)

R

```

Weird...just realized that was happening, it ran just fine in the inital RStudio window but I had the same issue in two different browsers.  However, for some reason it does work just fine if you put the shiny/map chunk first, and the bullets second. I have no idea why.

As for using leafletr, you need to create an html map first (example below). Then as long as that html file is in the same location as your Rmd file, and you aren't using any other shiny based chunks, you can simply reference that html in your Rmd, and write your entire Rmd file (or slides) to a html file. It embeds the html map into your slides (and seems to work fine with 2 column slide layouts). Bear in mind you do need internet to surf around a bit, but it's still stand-alone which is nice. leafletr is a little more involved than the basic leaflet package because it needs a spatial dataframe (points or polygons) to work, and it's best if reading from a geojson type file (you can always convert shapefiles, gpx, kmz, etc. to geojson). I tried to set up an example below so you can see this all in action. Let me know if you have questions, hopefully this works on your machine.  The Rmd file I used for all this is attached.

## leafletR example:
library(sp)
library(leafletR)
library(rgdal)

# make some data
df<-data.frame(long=seq(-121.8008,-121.8908,-0.0100),
               lat=seq(38.6295, 38.7195,0.0100), label=sprintf("Panel %d",1:10))

# designate your lat/longs
xy <- df[,c(1,2)]

# use rgdal to create spatial data frame (and add projection WGS84)
spdf <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(coords = xy,
                               data = df,
                               proj4string = CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +ellps=WGS84"))

# convert to GeoJSON (efficient storage of spatial data...can save data with webpage)
dfjson<-toGeoJSON(data=spdf, name="tst")

# now try making a leafletR map
map<-leaflet(data=dfjson, style=styleSingle(col="blue", fill.alpha=0.8),
             base.map=list("osm","tls"))
# view map
browseURL(map)

Adios,
R

messages.body_plain:
Hey Alex,

Looks like coplot() splits your conditional variable (fore_slope_ammended) into some arbitrary number of intervals that have some arbitrary amount of overlap. This is what function co.intervals() does, and the default for continuous conditional variables is to generate 6 intervals that overlap by 50% (see the help page for coplot)...in your plot, some of the data points in the different panels are the same. Once the intervals have been calculated, panel.car() plots the data points and optional linear regressions and loess smoothers. I am assuming that the function generates 6 data.frames that are subsets of the full dataset containing the data that falls into each interval for fore_slope_ammended, and then panel.car runs separate regressions (so, no full model with interactions and no mixed models).

The point of this whole thing seems to be visualizing statistical interactions. In this particular case, there does not seem to be much evidence for an interaction (the slopes are intercepts are qualitatively similar to my eye). Perhaps some of your other variables do show interactions, in which case it would be good to run models with statistical interactions (e.g. lm(log_DEA ~ daub_veg_H1_total_veg_cover * Fore_slope_ammended) )

I doubt there is an easy way to pull of the regression statistics using coplot. However, you should be able to use co.intervals and then run linear models on your own.

Here is an example using the quakes dataset (the one used in the help file for coplot):

Quakes coplot example
coplot( lat ~ long | depth, data = quakes )

What are the intervals being used?
with( quakes, co.intervals(depth) )   # using defaults, 6 intervals with 50% overlap
##       [,1]  [,2]
## [1,]  39.5 118.5
## [2,]  64.5 204.5
## [3,] 117.5 343.5
## [4,] 203.5 526.5
## [5,] 347.5 584.5
## [6,] 526.5 680.5

Save the intervals, use them to subset the quakes data.frame
int <- with( quakes, co.intervals(depth) )
quake.int <http://quake.int> <- list()
for(i in 1:nrow(int)){
     quake.int <http://quake.int>[[i]] <- quakes[quakes$depth >= int[i,1] & quakes$depth <= int[i,2],]
     }

Generate linear models – note, there are functions to do this (e.g. lmList in package nlme)
lm.int <http://lm.int> <- list()
for(i in 1:nrow(int)){
     lm.int <http://lm.int>[[i]] <- lm( lat~long, data=quake.int <http://quake.int>[[i]])
     }

Plot the data and add regression lines
par(mfrow=c(2,3))
for(i in 1:nrow(int)){
     plot( lat~long, quake.int <http://quake.int>[[i]] )
     abline( lm.int <http://lm.int>[[i]] )
     }

Pull regression coefficients into a matrix
matrix( unlist( lapply( lm.int <http://lm.int>, function(x) coef(x) )), ncol=2, byrow=T)
##            [,1]       [,2]
## [1,]   36.56873 -0.3212541
## [2,]   40.44535 -0.3415142
## [3,]   35.83966 -0.3144279
## [4,]   22.58533 -0.2415899
## [5,] -332.85617  1.7207225
## [6,]   33.40853 -0.2964758

I hope the helps some.

-Matt

messages.body_plain:
What about collapsing the list with bind_rows(), making it tidy, and then doing the merge?

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

df1 <- data.frame(id=1:6, area=c(7339, 7279, 7086, 7288, 7280, 7221),  CH4=2+runif(6))
df2 <- data.frame(id=7:12, area=c(7339, 7279, 7086, 7288, 7280, 7221),  CO2=2+runif(6))
df3 <- data.frame(id=13:18, area=c(7339, 7279, 7086, 7288, 7280, 7221),  NOX=2+runif(6))

target_df <- data.frame(id=1:18, col1=sample(letters, 18), col2=sample(LETTERS, 18))

l <- list(df1, df2, df3)

long_form <- l %>%
  bind_rows() %>% # Collapse the list into a data.frame. Use dplyr to allow different column names
  gather(key=gas, value=measurement, -id, -area) %>% # Convert to long form
  filter(!is.na <http://is.na>(measurement)) %>% # Only keep complete cases
  select(id, measurement) # Just pick out the id and measurement columns

final_df <- merge(target_df, long_form, by="id")

final_df

You can use the tidyr functions to ‘spread’ the data back out into short form (each gas will have its own column) after you’ve merged. I think I forgot to keep the ‘gas’ column in the filter() function call, so that is different in this script also.

Does this get you what you are looking for? Are there better ways for filtering out the NAs?

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

df1 <- data.frame(id=1:6, area=c(7339, 7279, 7086, 7288, 7280, 7221),  CH4=2+runif(6))

df2 <- data.frame(id=1:6, area=c(7339, 7279, 7086, 7288, 7280, 7221),  CO2=2+runif(6))

df3 <- data.frame(id=1:6, area=c(7339, 7279, 7086, 7288, 7280, 7221),  NOX=2+runif(6))

target_df <- data.frame(id=1:18, col1=sample(letters, 18), col2=sample(LETTERS, 18))

l <- list(df1, df2, df3)

long_form <- l %>%
  bind_rows() %>% # Collapse the list into a data.frame. Use dplyr to allow different column names
  gather(key=gas, value=measurement, -id, -area) %>% # Convert to long form
  filter(!is.na <http://is.na>(measurement)) %>% # Only keep complete cases

  select(id, gas, measurement) # Just pick out the id and measurement columns  ### FIRST DIFFERENCE

final_df <- merge(target_df, long_form, by="id") %>%
  spread(key = gas, value = measurement) ### SECOND DIFFERENCE

final_df

If you just want to get correlations between variables, I'd use the cor() function on your original dataset.

If you want to get the correlations between each variable and the principle component dimensions, access the $var slot of the fitted PCA object:

   > res.pca$var$cor             #apparently  this method only available for dimensions 1-5

The correlations between each variable and Dims 1 and 2 represent the (x,y) coordinate marking the endpoint of the variable's arrow on the biplot("Variables factor map"). For example, the tip of the arrow for '100m' is located at (-.775, .187) which are this variable's correlation with Dim.1 and Dim.2, respectively.

So in your dataset, the direction and length of the arrow for qn2oN indicates that it is strongly correlated with the first principle component axis (horizontal), and not at all correlated with the second component(vertical axis).

So what does that mean? I believe one way to think of it is that a substantial portion of the variation in your dataset (variation related to Dim/PC 1, 24%) is also related to variation in qn2oN (because the two are strongly correlated). In general, arrows which point the same direction in PCA-space tend to vary together within a dataset. In your case, it appears that WC, dist, qco2 appear to vary together, and kinda-vary with qn2oN

Note that your first two axes combined account for only 45% of the variation in the dataset so there are likely other dimensions (PC/Dim 3,4 etc) which also explain a lot of variation among the variables.

Hope I understood your question right. Maybe others can provide more accuracy / clarity?

Evening all,

I have a very complex dataset for which I have been advised I need to run an SEM. My problem is that I have not found any approaches that would allow for a hierarchical structure (e.g., lavaan requires no nesting or random effects).
I will start with a very simple description, and elaborate as needed.

Types of data:
1) Vegetation - functional group by percent cover, vertical cover (height), bare ground (%), litter (%)
2) Rodents - counts of unique captures, standardized by trapping effort
3) Snakes - counts of individuals, standardized by survey effort
4) Raptors - counts of individuals, standardized by survey effort
(It's a lot more complex than that, and the sample unit varies for each parameter, but I am not sure how much information is needed at this stage)

Other variables:
Location - we collected data at 4 locations (random effect)
Sites - there were 2 different site types within each of the 4 locations
Seasons - we collected data across 4 seasons

What we would like to do is somehow model the relationships between the four types of data, while accounting for site/location/season (if we don't account for these, I imagine we won't see anything interesting, but I could be wrong, because things like vegetation may help explain other trophic level responses more than "site type", but I am not sure).

Any leads or guidance would be greatly appreciated.

Happy Holidays!

Hi all,

This is my first time posting here. So thank you for your patience. I am trying to modify code from Richard’s statistical rethinking course to use with my own data (I am hoping some of you are familiar with this code). He provides code to run a Gaussian process model investigating spatial autocorrelation in Oceanic tools. In attempting to modify the code for my own data I have run into two issues.

First, in his example there is only one observation per island. With my data I have multiple observations per island (site) and need to modify the model to incorporate that. He explains how to do it in the book, but doesn’t actually provide the code. So, how can I modify the map2stan code to include multiple observations per island?

Second, the outcome variables in this example (total tools) are all positive integers. In my data, the outcome variables are the result of PCA, so are positive, negative and are not integers. Do I need to use a different distribution (besides poisson) for my data? Do you have any other thoughts on how to deal with this issue? Thanks so much and here is the code from Richard:

## R code 13.29

# load the distance matrix

library(rethinking)

data(islandsDistMatrix)

# display short column names, so fits on screen

Dmat <- islandsDistMatrix

colnames(Dmat) <- c("Ml","Ti","SC","Ya","Fi","Tr","Ch","Mn","To","Ha")

round(Dmat,1)

## R code 13.31

data(Kline2) # load the ordinary data, now with coordinates

d <- Kline2

d$society <- 1:10 # index observations

m13.7 <- map2stan(

    alist(

        total_tools ~ dpois(lambda),

        log(lambda) <- a + g[society] + bp*logpop,

        g[society] ~ GPL2( Dmat , etasq , rhosq , 0.01 ),

        a ~ dnorm(0,10),

        bp ~ dnorm(0,1),

        etasq ~ dcauchy(0,1),

        rhosq ~ dcauchy(0,1)

    ),

    data=list(

        total_tools=d$total_tools,

        logpop=d$logpop,

        society=d$society,

        Dmat=islandsDistMatrix),

    warmup=2000 , iter=1e4 , chains=4 )

## R code 13.32

precis(m13.7,depth=2)
